findings.title: Non-constant-time secret comparison and header injection risk
findings.body: The webhook secret check uses `!==` for comparison instead of a constant-time comparison function, which can leak timing information to attackers attempting to brute-force the secret. Additionally there's no rate limiting on this endpoint, making brute-force attacks on the webhook secret more feasible.

findings.title: Unhandled zod parse errors returns 500 instead of 400
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws if validation fails, but there's no try/catch or error handler around it, so malformed requests will cause an unhandled exception / 500 error rather than a clean 400 response.

findings.title: Decryption failures and malformed JSON not handled
findings.body: `symmetricDecrypt` and `JSON.parse` can both throw (e.g., wrong encryption key, corrupted payload, or no payload). There is no try/catch, so these errors will crash the handler and leak a generic 500 instead of a controlled error response. Also, if `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is unset, decryption proceeds with an empty string key silently.

findings.title: Credential uniqueness query doesn't guard against multiple user credentials for same app
findings.body: `findFirst` is used to locate an existing credential by `userId` and `appId`, but since a user can have multiple credentials for the same app type (as seen in other parts of this PR, e.g. office365video/zoom explicitly deleting duplicates), this could silently update the wrong credential, especially when a user has installed the same app more than once (e.g., team credentials vs personal).

findings.title: Minimum token schema always resolves to the last defined computed property
findings.body: `minimumTokenResponseSchema` defines two computed properties both using `z.string()`-based keys (`[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`), which because they are not literal strings evaluate to object keys like `"ZodString"`; this makes the intended "any numeric property is the expiry" and "other properties optional" catch-alls non-functional. The schema effectively never validates arbitrary extra keys as intended, so when `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is set, almost any response other than access_token-only objects will fail parsing, breaking refresh for self-hosted syncing.

findings.title: Credential sync endpoint called without authentication/secret
findings.body: The call to `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in a POST body but includes no authentication header, API key, or shared secret, even though a `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`/`CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` env var exists for the reverse direction (self-hoster → Cal.com). This endpoint can be impersonated or man-in-the-middled by anyone who knows (or guesses) the self-hoster's sync URL, allowing an attacker to retrieve access tokens for arbitrary `calcomUserId` values if the self-hosted endpoint doesn't do its own strict validation.

findings.title: Removed error logging path for invalid refreshed token responses
findings.body: The diff removes the `console.error` logging that reported the zodError and MS response when the refreshed token failed validation. Now failures silently fall through, making it much harder to diagnose refresh token failures in production, especially newly introduced via `parseRefreshTokenResponse` which can throw instead but the surrounding try/catch (if any) isn't shown here to handle that thrown error gracefully, risking an unhandled rejection and losing diagnostic context.

findings.title: Missing prisma import for new credential update call
findings.body: `CalendarService.ts` now calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` inside `getClient`, but the diff/file shown does not import `prisma` anywhere in this file (no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`). This will cause a reference error / fail to compile at runtime, breaking the Salesforce calendar refresh flow entirely.

findings.title: Salesforce token now refreshed on every service instantiation, ignoring expiry
findings.body: `getClient` previously likely used existing stored tokens unless expired; now it unconditionally calls the Salesforce OAuth refresh-token endpoint every time `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed, regardless of whether the current token is still valid. This causes unnecessary API calls per request/booking and could hit Salesforce rate limits, and discards the previously valid access token even when unnecessary refresh happens, which is a behavior change not called out in the PR description.
